name: Apache Solr
purpose: Mature Lucene-based search server with sharding, faceting, highlighting and a rich query DSL, run as a standalone service or a SolrCloud cluster.
journalism_use_case: The licence-clean index layer under a bespoke leak archive at multi-million-document scale: ICIJ's own extract/Datashare lineage targets Solr, so a newsroom can index millions of OCR'd pages and give reporters sub-second faceted search without Elastic's licence questions.
pros: Apache-2.0 end to end, so no repeat of the Elasticsearch relicensing problem that forced rework on several newsroom stacks
Proven at the document volumes investigative work actually hits; faceting and highlighting are first-class rather than bolted on
Schema, analysers and per-language text processing are explicit and auditable, which matters when you must explain why a reporter's search missed a document
ASF governance means releases, CVE handling and a long deprecation runway rather than a single vendor's roadmap
cons: No reporter-facing UI whatsoever — you must build one or front it with something like Blacklight, which is real engineering effort before a journalist sees value
Sharding, schema design and JVM/heap tuning need genuine operational expertise; a badly sized Solr is slower than a well-sized Postgres FTS

288 open issues and no GitHub 'latest release' object (releases are published via ASF channels and git tags such as releases/solr/10.1.0), so release tracking is less convenient than a GitHub-native project
ZooKeeper dependency for SolrCloud adds a second stateful system to operate
feedback: No newsroom-specific user reports were collected in this survey. The strongest documented deployment signal is architectural rather than anecdotal: ICIJ's extract pipeline targets Solr, and Blacklight-on-Solr is the standard pattern in library/archive projects. Treat as inference from project documentation, not a sourced testimonial.
assessment: For your profile this is a component, not a product: worth adopting if you are building a custom archive you expect to run for years and want zero licence ambiguity, and worth skipping if OpenAleph or Datashare already gives you the UI you need. The real cost is the front end. My judgement is that most small newsrooms should consume Solr indirectly (via Datashare/extract) and only stand it up directly when a bespoke schema or multi-tenant separation is the requirement.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest git tag releases/solr/10.1.0, 1,703 stars, 288 open issues. ASF project with formal release process and security mailing list. Judged active on substantive commit flow plus a current 10.x line, not on push recency alone.
licence_restrictions: None material. Permissive, patent grant included, safe to embed in a commercial newsroom product.
costs: No software fee. Cost is infrastructure plus operator time: a single-node index over a few million documents is comfortable on one 8-16GB-RAM VM plus SSD sized at roughly 30-50% of extracted text volume (estimate, assumptions: text-only index, no stored originals). SolrCloud with ZooKeeper triples the node count. Budget engineer time for schema design and an index-rebuild runbook; that labour, not licensing, is the dominant cost.
privacy: Fully self-hosted, no outbound calls, no telemetry in the core server. Residual risks are yours to manage: Solr admin APIs must never be exposed (historic RCE classes of bug exist in older versions), and query logs can themselves disclose what reporters are searching for, so log retention needs a policy.
alternatives: OpenSearch (Apache-2.0 fork of Elasticsearch, closer API compatibility with Aleph/Datashare defaults)
Datasette for anything that fits SQLite
OpenAleph if you want the whole archive product rather than an index
summary: Mature Lucene-based search server with sharding, faceting, highlighting and a rich query DSL…

name: Apache Tika
purpose: One API over roughly 1,400 file formats that detects type, extracts text and returns metadata, available as a Java library, a REST server (tika-server) and a CLI.
journalism_use_case: The format-coverage backbone of leak processing: a single call handles PDFs, legacy Office, RTF, Outlook PST/MSG, archives and images, and the metadata it returns (authors, creation timestamps, producing software, revision history) is frequently the story itself — as it was in document-provenance work on leaked memos.
pros: Format breadth no other single component matches, including the legacy and email formats that dominate real leaks and that modern Python-first parsers handle badly
Returns metadata as a first-class output, not an afterthought — critical for provenance questions about who made a document and when
Battle-tested as the extraction layer inside ICIJ extract, Datashare and the Aleph/OpenAleph ingest path, so your pipeline inherits a well-trodden route
Stable, versioned ASF releases with a long compatibility record, so pinning a version is realistic
cons: Extraction only: no layout model, no table structure, no reading-order reconstruction — a two-column scanned report comes out interleaved and you need Surya/Docling-class tooling on top
Parsing untrusted files in-process is a genuine security risk (parser CVEs are a recurring class); you must run tika-server sandboxed, which is extra architecture
JVM footprint and startup cost make it awkward inside lightweight Python workers; most teams end up running it as a service
No 'latest release' object exposed on GitHub (ASF distributes via dist.apache.org and git tags), so dependency tooling needs manual version tracking
feedback: No direct user reports collected. Documented deployment evidence is strong and verifiable from source: ICIJ extract and Datashare both declare Tika as the extraction dependency, which is a credible production signal at terabyte scale.
assessment: I would treat Tika as near-mandatory infrastructure rather than a choice, but always behind a sandbox. For your work the decisive property is that it is the only component that will not silently drop the ten-year-old .doc or the PST mailbox in a dump. Pair it with Dangerzone for anything from an unknown source, and do not expect it to solve layout — that is a separate stage.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, 4,153 stars, 64 open issues (low for a project this size, indicating issues are processed). ASF release process with a 2.x/3.x line and a security reporting channel. The low open-issue count relative to breadth is the strongest maintenance signal here.
licence_restrictions: None material; note that Tika bundles many third-party parsers whose own notices are aggregated in NOTICE.txt and must be reproduced if you redistribute.
costs: No software fee. Operating cost is a JVM service: 2-4GB RAM per tika-server instance plus CPU proportional to corpus size; OCR, if enabled through Tesseract, dominates compute. Infrastructure estimate only, assuming self-hosted containers.
privacy: Fully local processing; no network calls in the extraction path. The material privacy caveat is the inverse of the usual one — Tika extracts metadata you may not want to republish, so pair it with mat2 or an explicit scrubbing step before any document goes out.
alternatives: Unstructured (Python-native, narrower format coverage, licence caveats)
Docling for layout-aware parsing
libpff / libratom specifically for PST/email forensics
summary: One API over roughly 1,400 file formats that detects type, extracts text and returns metadata, available as a Java library…

name: Argos Translate
purpose: Offline neural machine translation library and CLI built on CTranslate2 and SentencePiece, with per-language-pair model packages installed as .argosmodel files.
journalism_use_case: Air-gapped batch translation of a document dump on an evidence machine: the Python API makes it straightforward to script gisting of thousands of foreign-language files so reporters can triage what needs professional human translation, with no API key and no text leaving the room.
pros: Genuinely offline after model download — the single most important property for leak material, and the reason it underpins LibreTranslate
Model packages are self-contained files you can stage onto an air-gapped machine, which is rare among MT stacks
MIT code with a small dependency surface (ctranslate2, sentencepiece, stanza), so it installs reliably and is easy to audit
Translation is fast enough on CPU for bulk triage, so no GPU budget is required
cons: Language coverage is narrower than NLLB or MADLAD, and many pairs route through English, compounding errors on e.g. Ukrainian→Arabic
Plain text and HTML only — no document-format preservation, so you lose the layout that often carries meaning in forms and filings
Quality on low-resource and dialectal material is well below commercial MT and below human usability for anything you intend to quote
The 'latest release' object on GitHub is v1.4.0 (2021) while the current tag is v1.11.0 — release metadata is inconsistent and versioning signals are weak
feedback: No individual user reports collected. The meaningful adoption signal is structural: LibreTranslate is built on Argos and has ~17.8k stars, which is secondary evidence that the engine works at service scale. Quality complaints on low-resource pairs are a known general property of OPUS-derived models rather than a specific documented issue I verified.
assessment: Use it as a triage instrument, never as a translation of record. For your context the right pattern is Argos (or LibreTranslate over it) for bulk gisting inside the perimeter, with a human translator for anything that reaches publication. Check the licence of each .argosmodel you install rather than assuming the MIT code licence covers the weights.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, 6,668 stars, 171 open issues, current tag v1.11.0 (GitHub's 'latest release' object is stale at v1.4.0 from 2021-08-24). Classified active on commit recency and tag progression; the stale release object and 171 open issues temper this — issue throughput looks thinner than commit activity.
model_or_data_licence: Per-package. Models derive from OPUS/OPUS-MT data and are mostly openly licensed, but terms vary by package and were NOT individually verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code is unrestricted. The uncertainty is at the weights layer: verify the specific .argosmodel package licence before relying on it for commercial publication.
costs: No fee. CPU-only operation on commodity hardware; each language pair is a few hundred MB of disk. Model downloads come from the Argos package index — one-time egress, then zero. Infrastructure estimate assuming a laptop or small VM.
privacy: No network calls at inference once models are present; the only network event is the initial package-index fetch, which you can perform on a separate machine and transfer. This makes it suitable for air-gapped evidence handling — an advantage LibreTranslate's public API does not have.
alternatives: LibreTranslate for a self-hosted HTTP endpoint over the same engine
Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT for direct HuggingFace control over specific pairs
CTranslate2 directly if you want to run NLLB/MADLAD-class models for better low-resource coverage
summary: Offline neural machine translation library and CLI built on CTranslate2 and SentencePiece…

name: BERTopic
purpose: Topic modelling pipeline that embeds documents, reduces dimensionality with UMAP, clusters with HDBSCAN and derives human-readable topic labels via class-based TF-IDF.
journalism_use_case: The strongest current answer to 'what is actually in this dump': cluster 200,000 leaked emails into a few hundred labelled themes, see which clusters are unexpected, and drill into those first instead of reading chronologically.
pros: Produces topic labels a reporter can read, which is what makes it usable in a newsroom where raw LDA output is not
Modular by design — you can swap in a local embedding model, so the whole pipeline stays offline
Strong documentation with worked examples for dynamic (over-time) and hierarchical topic modelling, both directly useful for narrative-change stories
Active release cadence and a 1.0 beta line, with the maintainer visibly responsive in the repo
cons: UMAP/HDBSCAN memory grows sharply past a few hundred thousand documents; at leak scale you need sampling, incremental fitting or a different approach, and this is the most common practical failure
Topic labels are statistical artefacts and over-merge or split in ways that mislead if taken at face value — every cluster needs human interpretation before it informs reporting
480 open issues suggests support load exceeds maintainer capacity, so expect to debug integration problems yourself
Results are sensitive to embedding model and UMAP random state; two runs can tell slightly different stories, which is awkward if you need a reproducible methodology note
feedback: No individual deployment reports verified. The 480 open issues against 7,963 stars is itself documented evidence of a single-maintainer project with heavy user demand. I did not verify any specific newsroom deployment, so treat journalism adoption as plausible rather than evidenced.
assessment: Genuinely useful for the triage problem, and I would pilot it on a real corpus before committing, specifically to measure the memory ceiling on your hardware. For your profile the key design decision is to fix the embedding model locally (e.g. multilingual-e5 via sentence-transformers) so no document text leaves the perimeter, and to record the random seed and model version in the methodology note so the clustering is reproducible if challenged.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.17.4 (2025-12-03) with a v1.0.0b1 tag since, 7,963 stars, 480 open issues. Active commits and a 1.0 beta in flight; the large open-issue backlog indicates responsiveness limits rather than abandonment.
model_or_data_licence: Depends entirely on the embedding model you choose; not fixed by BERTopic and not verified here.
licence_restrictions: None from BERTopic itself. The licence risk is imported with the embedding model — a CC-BY-NC checkpoint would contaminate commercial use.
costs: No fee. Embedding is the cost driver: a GPU shortens a 200k-document embedding run from many hours to tens of minutes. Expect a GPU VM for hours, or a long CPU run, per corpus. Estimate only; assumptions are a mid-size sentence-transformer and a single pass.
privacy: Local if and only if the embedding backend is local. Selecting an API-based embedding provider sends every document to a third party — a catastrophic default for leak material, and the one configuration choice that must be reviewed.
alternatives: txtai for a lighter all-in-one semantic search plus clustering
Carrot2 for labelling result sets rather than whole corpora
datasketch first, to collapse near-duplicates before topic modelling
summary: Topic modelling pipeline that embeds documents, reduces dimensionality with UMAP…

name: Buzz
purpose: Cross-platform desktop GUI over Whisper, whisper.cpp and faster-whisper that transcribes and translates audio and video files locally, exporting TXT, SRT and VTT.
journalism_use_case: The practical default for a reporter with no command line: drag a two-hour interview recording in, get a timestamped transcript and subtitles, with the audio never leaving the laptop. This is the tool that makes local transcription a newsroom policy rather than an engineering aspiration.
pros: Removes the engineering barrier entirely — installable app, no Python environment, which is what determines whether non-technical staff actually stop uploading interviews to cloud services
22,869 stars and only 20 open issues: an unusually healthy ratio indicating issues are actually closed
Wraps the faster-whisper/whisper.cpp backends, so you get near-state-of-the-art local accuracy without the reporter choosing a backend
Supports batch queues and subtitle export, covering the two things newsroom audio work actually needs
cons: Speaker diarisation is not a first-class feature, so multi-party interviews come out as undifferentiated text — the single biggest gap versus WhisperX or noScribe
Large models are slow on CPU; a reporter on a laptop without a GPU will wait, and may be tempted toward the cloud option
It ships an optional OpenAI API backend — a genuine foot-gun that uploads audio, and which needs an explicit newsroom policy or a locked-down build to prevent
Single-maintainer project; the bus factor is one
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The quantitative signal is unusually strong and checkable: 22.9k stars with 20 open issues on 2026-11-17 indicates both wide use and active triage — a better maintenance indicator than commit frequency alone.
assessment: This is the tool I would actually deploy to reporters, with the OpenAI backend disabled by policy or configuration and the gap on diarisation covered by sending multi-speaker material to a WhisperX or noScribe pipeline. Its value is social, not technical: it changes behaviour. For media-in-exile contexts where uploading an interview could identify a source, that behavioural change is the whole point.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v1.4.5 (2026-08-23), 22,869 stars, 20 open issues. Recent push, recent release and a near-empty issue tracker together justify 'actively maintained' rather than push-recency alone.
model_or_data_licence: Whisper, whisper.cpp and faster-whisper weights are MIT. The optional OpenAI API mode uses a hosted model under OpenAI's terms instead.
licence_restrictions: None material for the local path.
costs: Free. Note the project also distributes a paid App Store build on some platforms as a convenience — the GitHub release is free. Real cost is reporter wait time on CPU; a modest GPU workstation shared by the newsroom removes it. If the OpenAI backend is enabled you incur per-minute API charges — verify current rates at point of use; not priced here.
privacy: Local by default: audio is processed on the machine and nothing is uploaded. The exception is explicit and must be managed — selecting the OpenAI Whisper API backend sends the audio to OpenAI. For source protection, disable or remove that option and document the decision.
alternatives: noScribe where speaker-labelled interview transcripts and a correction editor are the priority
WhisperX for engineer-run pipelines needing diarisation and word-level timing
Subtitle Edit for caption production rather than transcription
summary: Cross-platform desktop GUI over Whisper, whisper.cpp and faster-whisper that transcribes and translates audio and video files…

name: Camelot
maintainer: camelot-dev community (fork of the archived atlanhq/camelot)
purpose: Python library that extracts tables from born-digital PDFs using two strategies — lattice (ruling-line detection) and stream (whitespace clustering) — and returns pandas DataFrames with a per-table accuracy score.
journalism_use_case: Pulling budget tables, campaign-finance schedules and procurement annexes out of text-layer PDFs into spreadsheets at scale. The per-table accuracy score is the underrated feature: it tells a reporter which of 400 extracted tables need manual checking, turning an unbounded verification task into a ranked one.
pros: The accuracy/whitespace score per table is a genuine auditability feature — few extractors tell you how confident they are
Two complementary algorithms cover both ruled and unruled tables, which between them handle most government PDF conventions
Community fork is demonstrably alive (v2.0.0 released 2026-06-04) after the original atlanhq repo went dead — the licence and lineage are clean
Outputs straight to pandas/CSV, so it drops into an existing data-journalism workflow with no glue
cons: Requires a real text layer: scanned pages must be OCR'd first (OCRmyPDF), and this trips people up constantly
Merged cells, tables spanning page breaks and rotated pages all degrade output; multi-page financial annexes usually need custom stitching code
Ghostscript and OpenCV dependencies make the install heavier than pdfplumber's
The widely-linked original repo (atlanhq/camelot) is dead, so most search results and old Stack Overflow answers point at the wrong project — a real practical trap
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented community signal is the fork itself: the move from atlanhq to camelot-dev, with a 2.0.0 release in 2026, is evidence of a user base large enough to rescue the project. 3,857 stars, 58 open issues.
assessment: Keep both Camelot and pdfplumber installed and choose per document — Camelot when the table has ruling lines and you want a confidence score, pdfplumber when you need character coordinates and a visual debugger. For your work the accuracy score is what justifies Camelot's extra install weight: it lets you build a pipeline that escalates low-confidence tables to a human rather than silently publishing a mis-parsed budget figure.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v2.0.0 (2026-06-04), 3,857 stars, 58 open issues. A major version in 2026 plus current commits on a community fork; classified active on release substance, not push recency.
licence_restrictions: None material. Note Ghostscript is a runtime dependency and is AGPL-licensed when obtained from Artifex without a commercial licence — relevant if you redistribute a bundled product, not for internal use.
costs: No fee. CPU-only, negligible infrastructure. The real cost is engineer time writing per-document-family extraction rules and the human review of low-confidence tables. Ghostscript licensing could become a cost if you ship Camelot inside a commercial product.
privacy: Fully local; no network calls. Safe for sensitive documents on an isolated machine.
alternatives: pdfplumber for coordinate-level control and visual debugging
Tabula for a no-code reporter-driven workflow
Surya/Marker or Docling for scanned or complex-layout tables where neither Camelot strategy applies
summary: Python library that extracts tables from born-digital PDFs using two strategies…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: Carrot2
purpose: Search-results clustering engine that groups a result set into labelled thematic clusters, with Java and REST interfaces and connectors for Solr and Elasticsearch.
journalism_use_case: Attaches human-readable cluster labels to a search over a document archive, so a reporter who queries a leak for a company name sees the thematic shape of 3,000 hits — contracts, litigation, internal complaints — instead of a flat ranked list.
pros: Designed for the exact newsroom problem of too many search hits, and produces short noun-phrase labels rather than word clouds
Drops in behind an existing Solr or Elasticsearch index, so it is an incremental addition rather than a new system
Licence question resolved in this survey: the open engine is a genuine BSD-style licence read from carrot2.LICENSE, not a restricted core
Steady releases (release/4.8.6, 2026-03-08) from a commercial sponsor with a long track record
cons: Designed to cluster result sets of hundreds to a few thousand documents, not an entire corpus — it complements topic modelling rather than replacing it
The higher-quality Lingo3G algorithm is a separate commercial product not in this repository, so the open version is deliberately the weaker tier
JVM-only; awkward in a Python-centric stack except via the REST service
Small community (859 stars, 17 open issues) means limited third-party examples and little journalism-specific documentation
feedback: No user reports collected. The commercial-sponsor model (open core plus paid Lingo3G) is documented on the vendor site and is the key structural fact to understand; I did not verify Lingo3G pricing, which is not publicly listed in machine-readable form.
assessment: A narrow, well-executed tool that earns its place only if you already run Solr or Elasticsearch over a corpus reporters search interactively. For your profile I would treat it as an optional UX improvement rather than a core component, and I would check whether BERTopic over the result set gives you enough without adding a JVM service. The open/commercial split is honest but means you are using the deliberately lesser algorithm.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release release/4.8.6 (2026-03-08), 859 stars, 17 open issues. GitHub's SPDX field is null and the licence was read from the repository's own carrot2.LICENSE file. Commits continue and issues are few; this is a mature component with modest change velocity rather than a declining one.
licence: BSD-3-Clause-style (custom Carrot2 BSD-style text read directly from carrot2.LICENSE; GitHub SPDX null)
licence_restrictions: Open engine is permissive. The restriction is commercial rather than legal: the best clustering algorithm (Lingo3G) is not included and requires a paid licence from Carrot Search — price not publicly listed, quote required.
costs: Open engine free. Lingo3G is a separate paid product with no public price list (quote required; not verified). Infrastructure: a small JVM service alongside your index. Estimate only.
privacy: Fully local when self-hosted; clustering happens on your result sets with no outbound calls. If you use the hosted Carrot Search demo service instead, your queries and documents go to a third party — avoid for sensitive corpora.
alternatives: BERTopic for corpus-level topic discovery
txtai for semantic search plus clustering in one Python dependency
Solr's own clustering component for a lighter integration
summary: Search-results clustering engine that groups a result set into labelled thematic clusters…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: CTranslate2
purpose: C++/Python inference engine for transformer models with aggressive quantisation (int8, int16, float16), used to run translation and speech models far faster and smaller than the reference PyTorch implementations.
journalism_use_case: The engine that makes offline AI practical on newsroom hardware: int8 quantisation lets a 600M-1.3B translation model or Whisper large run on a CPU laptop instead of a cloud API, which is what turns 'we should process this locally' into something that actually finishes before deadline.
pros: The quantisation story is the decisive capability — it changes the hardware class needed, and therefore whether local processing is viable at all for a small newsroom
Powers faster-whisper and Argos/LibreTranslate, so its reliability is already proven in the tools your reporters would use
Active releases (v4.9.0, 2026-11-10) with CPU and CUDA backends maintained in parallel
Small, dependency-light C++ core that you can actually build and audit
cons: Engineer-facing only: no UI, no file handling, and you must convert the model yourself with the source framework installed
Quantisation costs measurable quality, and the loss is model- and language-dependent, so you need to evaluate rather than assume
276 open issues, and CUDA/cuDNN version mismatches are a recurring install failure that you will debug
Supports a specific set of architectures — a new model family is not guaranteed to be convertible
feedback: No individual user reports collected. Strong indirect evidence: faster-whisper (26.8k stars) and the Argos/LibreTranslate line both depend on CTranslate2, which is verifiable from their dependency declarations and constitutes real production use.
assessment: For your profile this is foundational plumbing rather than a tool you use directly: you will meet it through faster-whisper and Argos. Install it directly when you need to run a specific translation model (NLLB, MADLAD) that no wrapper exposes, or when you need to squeeze a model onto field hardware. Budget evaluation time to measure the quantisation quality loss on your actual languages — do not accept it on faith.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-10, latest release v4.9.0 published the same day (2026-11-10), 4,755 stars, 276 open issues. A same-day push and release is a clear active signal; the open-issue count reflects breadth of hardware/driver combinations rather than neglect.
model_or_data_licence: Engine only. Converted weights retain the licence of the source model — converting a CC-BY-NC checkpoint does not make it permissive.
licence_restrictions: None from the engine. The frequent error is assuming the MIT engine licence launders a restricted model licence; it does not.
costs: No fee. The point of the project is to reduce infrastructure cost: CPU-only int8 inference on existing laptops versus GPU rental. Optional CUDA path needs a GPU. Estimate; assumes self-hosted.
privacy: Entirely local, no telemetry, no network. One of the cleanest privacy profiles in the catalogue and the basis for the local-first transcription and translation stack.
alternatives: llama.cpp / whisper.cpp for GGUF-based local inference
ONNX Runtime / sherpa-onnx for mobile and locked-down devices
vLLM when you have GPUs and need throughput over footprint
summary: C++/Python inference engine for transformer models with aggressive quantisation (int8, int16, float16)…
oss_detail: Open-source code, data or models you load carrying their own terms, some non-commercial

name: Datasette
purpose: Web application that serves one or more SQLite databases as a browsable, queryable, JSON-API-exposed website, with a large plugin ecosystem and publishing subcommands.
journalism_use_case: The fastest route from 'we have extracted the leak into a table' to 'reporters can search it': point Datasette at a SQLite file of document text and metadata and the team has faceted search, saved queries and CSV export within an hour. Also the standard way to publish a cleaned subset alongside a story so readers can check the data themselves.
pros: Time-to-usefulness is unmatched in this catalogue — a single command turns a file into a shared research tool, which is decisive under deadline
Plugin ecosystem (datasette-search-all, full-text search, cluster maps, graphs) covers most newsroom asks without custom code
Read-only by design, so handing reporters a URL cannot corrupt the dataset — a genuine safety property in a shared investigation
Exceptional documentation and an articulated data-journalism design philosophy; the maintainer is embedded in this community
cons: SQLite FTS is excellent for structured extracts but is not a substitute for a sharded index over millions of full documents — it will not replace Solr/Elasticsearch at leak scale

The publish subcommands intentionally push data to third-party hosts (Vercel, Cloud Run, Fly); running one against unvetted data is a one-command leak, and that risk sits right next to the normal workflow
666 open issues across the core project and a long-running 1.0 alpha line, so the stable release (0.65.x) and the alpha (1.0a43) diverge and plugin compatibility needs checking
Read-only means annotation, tagging and collaborative review must live in another tool
feedback: No individual reports verified, but Datasette's role in data journalism is documented by the project itself and by its plugin ecosystem's orientation (publishing, mapping, CSV export). 11,590 stars, 666 open issues. I did not verify specific newsroom deployments, so treat named-outlet claims as unestablished.
assessment: I would adopt this immediately and keep it permanently in the toolkit — it is the lowest-effort, highest-return item in the document pillar. The one governance rule I would write down: `datasette publish` is forbidden on any database derived from source material, because the gap between 'share internally' and 'upload to a public host' is a single subcommand. Pair with a real search engine for full-document scale.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 0.65.6 (2026-11-15), current tag 1.0a43, 11,590 stars, 666 open issues. Frequent point releases on the stable line plus an in-progress 1.0; the open-issue count is large but the release cadence is the stronger signal.
licence_restrictions: None material; permissive and safe for commercial publishing products.
costs: No fee. Self-hosting is trivially cheap (a small VM or container). If you use the publish path to a commercial PaaS you pay that provider's rates — verify at point of use; not priced here. Operating effort is low, which is much of the value.
privacy: Local and self-hostable with no outbound calls in normal operation. The explicit exception is the publishing subcommands, which are designed to move data off-premises; treat them as a separate, policy-controlled action rather than part of the analysis workflow.
alternatives: Apache Solr or OpenSearch for full-document scale
VisiData for terminal-based exploration of the same data
DuckDB plus a notebook where analysis rather than sharing is the goal
summary: Web application that serves one or more SQLite databases as a browsable, queryable, JSON-API-exposed website…

name: datasketch
purpose: Probabilistic data-structure library providing MinHash, MinHash LSH, LSH Forest, Weighted MinHash, HyperLogLog and LSH Ensemble for sub-linear similarity search over large sets.
journalism_use_case: Deduplicating a leak before anyone reads it: collapse thousands of near-identical email chains, repeated attachments and boilerplate contracts into representative clusters, so a reporting team reads 40,000 distinct documents instead of 200,000 mostly-redundant ones.
pros: Solves the single highest-leverage preprocessing problem in leak work — redundancy — and does so at a scale where exact comparison is impossible
MinHash LSH with Redis or Cassandra backing lets the index persist and grow across ingest batches rather than being rebuilt
Small, well-documented, dependency-light (NumPy), and easy to reason about when you must defend the methodology
Steady releases (v2.0.0, 2026-07-05) and 2,980 stars with a manageable issue count
cons: Approximate by design: thresholds must be tuned and will produce false pairs, so a human-visible review step is mandatory before anything is discarded
Shingling choices (word vs character n-grams, size) materially change results, and there is no newsroom-oriented guidance on picking them
No document-level UI or report — you are building the dedup workflow around it
Says nothing about which duplicate is canonical; provenance decisions (which copy is the evidence of record) are entirely yours
feedback: No user reports collected. 2,980 stars with 71 open issues on 2026-11-17 indicates a stable, maintained library with modest support load. No journalism-specific deployment verified.
assessment: Unglamorous and high value: deduplication is where leak processing time is actually won or lost, and this is the right primitive for it. For your profile I would wire it into ingest immediately after text extraction, keep every duplicate (never delete — mark and cluster), and record the shingle and threshold parameters as part of the corpus methodology so a later challenge can be answered.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-26, latest release v2.0.0 (2026-07-05), 2,980 stars, 71 open issues. A 2.0 release in 2026 plus commits within the last month; low-churn library behaviour, judged active on release substance.
costs: No fee. CPU-only and cheap; memory scales with the number of hashed documents. A persistent LSH index adds a Redis instance. Infrastructure estimate only.
privacy: Fully local. If you configure a Redis or Cassandra backend, the hashes (not the documents) live there — still treat that store as sensitive, since MinHash signatures over a confidential corpus are themselves disclosive about its contents.
alternatives: ImageHash / imagededup for the same problem on images
RapidFuzz for short-string rather than document-level similarity
Splink where the goal is record linkage with probabilities rather than near-duplicate collapse
summary: Probabilistic data-structure library providing MinHash, MinHash LSH, LSH Forest, Weighted MinHash…
